blocks.text: f) Hamid says: "I will make the allowance 20% next year, just to be safe." Evaluate this idea. (3)

For: a bigger allowance is more cautious, so assets and profit are less likely to be overstated.
Against: the allowance must be a reasonable estimate based on past experience. 20% is far above Hamid's real losses, so profit and trade receivables would be understated and the statements would not be reliable. A sudden change also breaks the consistency concept.
Conclusion: keep a realistic rate (about 5%) and change it only when experience of bad debts changes. Prudence means do not overstate; it does not mean understate on purpose.

blocks.text: e) Kwame wants to change to the reducing balance method in 2026 so his profit looks higher. Advise him, naming the concept involved. (3)

The consistency concept says Kwame should use the same depreciation method every year.
He may change only if the new method gives a fairer view of how the vans lose value, and he must explain the change.
Changing just to make profit look higher would mislead users and stop them comparing this year with earlier years. He should not change.

Concepts
The ten accounting concepts and the inventory valuation rule.

rows: The business is separate from its owner.
Owner's private house is not recorded; goods taken are drawings.
Every transaction has two equal effects: a debit and a credit.
Buy equipment by cheque: equipment up, bank down.
Only record items with a money value.

Question 12.16 (Level 2: Easy to medium)
For each situation, name the concept which applies and explain how it applies. (2 marks each)
a) The owner paid for a family holiday with a business cheque. It was recorded as drawings.
The holiday is a private expense of the owner. The business is separate from the owner, so the payment is drawings, not a business expense.
b) Goods were sold on credit on 29 December 2025 and paid for on 5 January 2026. The sale was recorded in 2025.
Revenue is recorded when the goods pass to the customer (29 December 2025), not when the cash is received.
c) A waste bin costing RM8 was recorded as an expense, although it will last for years.
RM8 is too small to affect any user's decision. Treating it as a non-current asset and depreciating it is not worth the effort.
d) Premises bought for RM80,000 are now worth RM120,000. They are still shown at RM80,000.
Assets are recorded at the price paid. Cost is objective and backed by documents; the RM120,000 is only an estimate.

Question 12.18 (Level 4: Hard)
Mira made the decisions below. For each one, name the concept she has not followed, explain why, and state the correct treatment. (3 marks each)
a) She changed her depreciation method from straight line to reducing balance this year. She plans to change back next year to make her profit look steady.

Why: switching methods to smooth profit makes the years impossible to compare and misleads users.
Correct treatment: choose the method that suits the asset and use it every year. Change only for a good reason and explain the change.
b) She recorded the repayment of her personal car loan as a business expense.

Why: the car loan is the owner's private debt, not the business's.
Correct treatment: record the payment as drawings.
c) She included in 2025 revenue an order received on 28 December 2025 for goods to be delivered in February 2026.

Why: the goods have not passed to the customer, so the revenue has not been earned.
Correct treatment: record the sale in February 2026 when the goods are delivered.
d) She did not record December electricity of RM400 because the bill had not been paid.

Why: the electricity was used in 2025, so it is a 2025 expense even though it is unpaid.
Correct treatment: add RM400 to the electricity expense and show RM400 in other payables (current liabilities).
e) She increased the value of premises from cost of RM100,000 to a market value of RM150,000 and added the RM50,000 to profit.

Why: premises must stay at cost. The RM50,000 gain has not been earned by a sale (prudence and realisation also apply).
Correct treatment: keep premises at RM100,000 and do not add RM50,000 to profit.

Question 12.19 (Level 5: Challenge)
A business is thinking of closing down. The following information is available.
If the business closes, RM10,500 is the amount of trade receivables expected to be collected.
a) Calculate net assets on the going concern basis (book values). (3)
b) Calculate net assets if the business closes. (3)

rows: Total assets if the business closes (RM)
Net assets if the business closes (RM)

blocks.text: c) Explain why the two figures are different. Name the concept involved. (3)

Going concern assumes the business will continue, so assets are shown at cost less depreciation because they will be used, not sold. If the business closes, assets must be valued at what they would raise now. Equipment and inventory sold quickly fetch much less, so net assets fall by RM5,900.
d) While the business continues trading, premises must stay at RM80,000 even though they are worth RM95,000. Name two concepts that support this. (2)
e) Name two users of the financial statements who would be interested in these figures, and give a reason for each. (2)

Any two, with a reason:
Owner: to decide whether to close or keep trading.
Bank or lender: to see whether the RM25,000 loan will be repaid.
Suppliers (trade payables): to see whether they will be paid.
Employees: to judge whether their jobs are safe.
